evals.prompt: I'm the founder of Trellisway. We maintain an Apache-2.0 workflow engine: teams write DAGs in Python, our server schedules and retries them, keeps run history, ships a web UI. Opt-in telemetry says roughly 9,400 self-hosted installs, 58% of them inside companies. There are five of us, 14 months of runway, and revenue is exactly zero. Two of us came out of SRE; nobody here has ever sold anything in their life. We need to turn this into an actual business. What's the move?
evals.expected_output: A constraint statement, an explicit pass over the archetype space with each rejection carrying a blocking reason, a stated efficiency ranking, two or three candidate models each with a dated validation experiment, and a single recommended primary with its go-to-market consequence.
expectations: States the licence position as a fixed constraint before proposing any model, noting that the Apache-2.0 releases already published stay licensed that way permanently
States where the software runs today (customer-side, self-hosted) as a fixed constraint
States who would sign the contract, distinguishing the DAG author from the engineering or platform leader who buys
Walks the archetype space and marks options as possible, blocked, or premature instead of jumping straight to a single answer
Rejects dual licensing and names the permissive Apache-2.0 licence, which creates no forcing function, as the blocking constraint
Rejects an ecosystem take-rate and names the absence of two-sided liquidity as the blocking constraint
Presents two or three candidate models, never only one
States the ranking order explicitly in the text rather than leaving it implied by the order candidates happen to be listed in
Ranks candidates by value returned per unit of founder effort rather than by which is cheapest or easiest to start
Gives each candidate a validation experiment carrying both a named success criterion and a date
Commits to exactly one primary model with at most one secondary, and never leaves two primaries standing
Names the go-to-market consequence of the recommended model: the motion it forces and the functions that must be built or hired

evals.prompt: Sanity check on our paid tier before we announce it. Nuvexa is an MIT-licensed feature-flag server; about 2,000 organizations self-host it. We're putting the following behind the Enterprise plan: SAML/SSO login, role-based access control, audit logging, the Kubernetes operator (which honestly was written by a contributor at a bank, not by us), and bulk CSV export of flag history. Everything else stays free exactly as it is. Does that boundary hold?
evals.expected_output: A rewritten boundary that removes SSO, the community-built operator and data export from the paid side while keeping the governance surface, with all five paid-boundary tests answered in writing and any failure treated as blocking.
expectations: Removes SAML/SSO from the paid side and refuses to treat it as an acceptable enterprise gate
Cites sso.tax or the sso-wall-of-shame catalogue, or its argument that security should not be a premium feature, when rejecting paid SSO
Removes the community-contributed Kubernetes operator from the paid side
Names the hostile fork as the consequence of selling contributors their own work back to them
Removes bulk CSV export of flag history from the paid side because data export must not be gated
Keeps role-based access control and audit logging as legitimate organization-only paid surface
Applies the organization-only test: everything paid must be something a company needs and a solo developer does not
Applies the defensibility test by asking whether a motivated contributor could rebuild the paid part upstream in a weekend and would want to
Applies the observable-trigger test and names a concrete, visible signal that a user has crossed from free need to paid need
Applies the cost-to-serve test and asks what one free user costs per month in currency
Applies the licence-compatibility test against the MIT licence already published
Treats a failed test as blocking rather than as a weakness to be offset by strengths elsewhere
Answers the five tests in writing, one by one, rather than closing with an overall impression of the boundary

evals.prompt: Can you fill in a business model canvas for us? The product is Lanternctl, a Go CLI for managing edge device fleets, BSD-licensed, public for two years. Just do the nine boxes please: key partners, key activities, value propositions, customer relationships, customer segments, key resources, channels, cost structure, revenue streams. I'm taking it to the board on Thursday.
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the canvas as the first deliverable, naming the three inputs it never asks for, followed by the constraint, archetype and paid-boundary work, with the canvas offered afterwards if still wanted.
expectations: Declines to fill the nine boxes as the first deliverable and explains why before producing anything
Names the licence already published as something the canvas never asks about
Names where the software runs as a second input the canvas leaves out
Names whether any paid boundary can hold as a third input the canvas leaves out
Runs the constraint, archetype-space and paid-boundary work in place of the canvas
Treats the BSD licence on already-released versions as permanent and unchangeable
Offers to produce the canvas afterwards if the user still wants it, rather than refusing outright
Does not invent revenue-stream figures or customer-segment sizes in order to populate boxes
Asks about the buyer and the deployment reality instead of assuming them

evals.prompt: I need a number from you. Kestrelbase sells an observability agent. The free open-source agent is everywhere, and the paid tier unlocks multi-tenant RBAC, retention policies and SOC 2 compliance reporting. We list it at $39 per seat per month with a Stripe checkout right on the pricing page. At what annual contract value should we stop doing self-serve and hire an inside sales rep, and at what number do we need a real field sales team? Give me the thresholds.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to invent currency thresholds, a unit-economics model of the sale with the Skok reference points attributed and labelled SaaS-wide, and identification of the enterprise-boundary-priced-as-self-serve mismatch with its two fixes.
expectations: Refuses to give currency thresholds separating self-serve from inside sales from field sales, and says no defensible published bands exist
Offers to derive the answer from the company's own cohort data instead of a published band
Models the sale with unit economics: estimated lifetime value against estimated acquisition cost, plus the months needed to earn the acquisition cost back
Quotes the lifetime-value-to-acquisition-cost guideline of higher than 3, and as high as 7 or 8 in the best businesses
Quotes the guideline that acquisition cost is recovered in 5-7 months
Attributes both reference points to David Skok's SaaS Metrics 2.0
Labels both reference points as describing SaaS generally rather than developer tools specifically
Identifies the mismatch between a paid boundary that only triggers at enterprise governance needs and a self-serve credit-card motion
Explains that the cost of a sale carrying security review, procurement and legal eats a per-seat contract of this size
Offers both fixes: move the boundary down so a small team crosses it, or price and staff for the sale the boundary actually requires
Treats a candidate that cannot plausibly reach those reference points as a motion problem to fix before committing, not as a revenue forecast

evals.prompt: Halyard is our Apache-2.0 distributed queue. Two weeks ago a major cloud provider launched 'Managed Halyard': same API, their console, their pricing, and their sales team is already sitting in two of our biggest users' accounts. The board wants us to ship the next release under BUSL-1.1 and put out a blog post announcing our new open source licence. What do we do?
evals.expected_output: Treatment of the licence change as an irreversible lever sequenced on the reversibility ladder, corrected naming discipline, documented precedent, and a requirement to name the model the licence protects and to run the reversible experiment first.
expectations: Treats a licence change on published code as effectively irreversible and separates it from the reversible decisions
States that every Apache-2.0 release already published stays licensed that way forever, whatever the next release ships under
Refuses to call BUSL-1.1 open source and supplies source-available, fair source or delayed open source as the correct term
Cites the OSI ruling that SSPL violates the Open Source Definition, or Bruce Perens' objection to restrictive licences being called open source, when explaining the naming discipline
Cites at least one documented relicensing outcome by name: Elasticsearch and the OpenSearch fork, Redis and the Valkey fork, or HashiCorp and the OpenTofu fork
Notes that every documented relicensing has produced a fork, a trust cost, or both
Places the source-available decision on the reversibility ladder rather than ranking it as a tenth peer archetype
States that source-available creates no buyer of its own and only protects whichever model sits underneath it
Requires the model the licence change is meant to protect to be named and chosen before the licence moves
Runs the reversible experiment first to buy evidence before pulling the irreversible lever
Names contributor count and downstream packaging status as what to watch in the quarters after a change
Names the distributions, foundations, corporate allowlists or procurement processes that exclude non-OSI licences

evals.prompt: Two of us just went full time on Pipesmith, an MIT-licensed data-transform library with about 400,000 monthly downloads. Here's the revenue plan: GitHub Sponsors with $5, $25 and $100 tiers, a $6/month 'Pipesmith Pro' badge for individual developers who want to support us, and we'll take consulting gigs implementing Pipesmith at companies when they come in. Sanity check the plan, anything we're missing?
evals.expected_output: A verdict that none of the three lines is a company model, with donations routed to funding-side guidance, consulting allowed only as a bridge, individuals recast as the adoption base, and at least one archetype proposed that an organization would actually sign.
expectations: States that sponsorship and donations sustain maintainers rather than payroll, and are not a company revenue model
Routes the sponsorship question to dedicated funding-side guidance instead of counting sponsor income as revenue in the model
States that consulting and implementation services cap growth at hiring speed
Allows consulting as a bridge while rejecting it as a destination
Treats individual developers as the adoption and credibility base rather than the revenue base
Notes that individuals pay small amounts for convenience and churn fast
Names organizations as the revenue base and what they actually buy: risk removal, uptime, support, compliance, control, someone to call
Proposes at least one archetype monetizing an organization that signs, instead of only repackaging the individual tiers
Names the buyer inside that organization and what would make them sign
Names the moment a user acquires a reason to pay, rather than assuming goodwill converts into revenue

evals.prompt: Context on Ferrolane before you answer. Our engine is AGPL-3.0 and every contributor has signed our CLA since day one, so we own the copyright outright. Three of our four engineers are ex-SRE and we already run a small hosted instance for two design partners. The board wants a signed paying customer before the quarter closes, so twelve weeks. We have nobody who could build metering and billing this year, and no support rota at all. Give me the model ranking.
evals.expected_output: A ranking re-ranked against this company's specific advantages and constraints, with dual licensing promoted for the AGPL-plus-CLA prerequisite, hosted models promoted for the existing operations function, four archetypes deleted with named reasons, and each move traced to the answer that caused it.
expectations: Re-ranks the default order against this company's own situation instead of presenting a generic ordering
Promotes dual licensing toward the top and names AGPL-3.0 plus full copyright ownership under a signed CLA as the reason
Promotes hosted models because the team already operates a service, so the expensive function is already paid for
Deletes consumption metering and names the absence of billing engineering as the cause
Deletes support and LTS and names the absence of a support rota as the cause
Deletes embedded OEM licensing because it cannot produce revenue inside a twelve-week window
Deletes the ecosystem take-rate because it cannot produce revenue inside a twelve-week window
Deletes ruled-out options outright rather than parking them lower in the ranking
States which answer moved which option, instead of presenting the re-ranked order without its reasons
Warns that the ordering is a default rather than a law
Names a commercial-licence enquiry page with counted inbound as the cheap validation test for dual licensing

evals.prompt: Quick one on Braidmark, our schema-migration service. We bill $30 per developer seat per month. The problem: seat count has been flat for three quarters while API calls tripled, mostly because customers wired us into CI and into coding agents that open migrations automatically. Finance wants to add a per-API-call charge on top of the seat price, same accounts, keep both. Thoughts?
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that seats collapse under automation, a refusal to stack consumption on top of seats for the same value, the four value-metric checks applied to a replacement metric, and consumption guardrails plus the right leading indicator.
expectations: States that per-seat pricing collapses when usage grows through automation and agents instead of headcount
Rejects stacking a consumption charge and seats on the same underlying value
Explains that billing both makes the customer optimise against the vendor
Tests any candidate metric against whether the customer already counts it for their own reasons
Tests whether the metric grows as the value the customer receives grows
Tests whether the customer can forecast the metric before the invoice arrives
Tests whether the vendor can measure the metric accurately and explain the measurement in one sentence
Rejects a metric only the vendor can measure, because it turns every invoice into a dispute
Requires spend caps, alerts or forecasting before any consumption billing ships
Names bill shock as the failure mode consumption billing dies of, and public posts from a developer audience as how it surfaces
Names net revenue retention, or the share of accounts above a committed floor, as the leading indicator for a metered model

evals.prompt: An investor asked about our free tier last week and I fumbled it badly. Cindersync is a hosted sync service for mobile apps. The free plan gives 50 GB of stored data, unlimited devices and unlimited bandwidth, which we think is pretty generous, and it is genuinely driving all of our signups. Paid starts at $99/month. How do I defend the free tier next time someone asks?
evals.expected_output: A requirement to quantify the marginal cost of a free user in currency, identification of the infrastructure-heavy free surfaces, caps on those dimensions, and the verdict that a cost-to-serve failure means the wrong value metric.
expectations: Requires the marginal cost of one free user to be computed in currency rather than described as generous
States that a free tier described in adjectives rather than numbers is an untested model
Identifies unlimited bandwidth and 50 GB of stored data as infrastructure-heavy free surface that makes growth actively expensive
Notes that heavy per-user infrastructure cost rules out generous free tiers of any kind
Recommends caps, quotas or metering on the infrastructure-heavy dimensions
Also asks what one paying customer costs to serve, not only the free user
Treats a model failing the cost-to-serve check as having the wrong value metric rather than needing more discipline
Requires the free-versus-paid line to be defensible on organization-only grounds rather than on volume alone
Reports the cost-to-serve result inside an explicit threshold check rather than as a passing remark

evals.prompt: We've picked our model. Runnelgraph stays fully Apache-2.0 and we sell the managed service around it. Now I want the internal one-pager so the team can execute without me in the room. We'll track MRR and GitHub stars monthly so we know it's working, and for the risk section I have competition, execution and market timing. Write it up properly please.
evals.expected_output: A memo with the named sections, MRR and stars replaced by an indicator upstream of revenue with a target, a date and a margin guardrail, each risk given an observable signal, at least three revisit triggers including a failure condition, and section-by-section agreement rather than a single dump.
expectations: Rejects monthly recurring revenue as a leading indicator because revenue is the outcome rather than something upstream of it
Rejects GitHub stars because they measure attention that no model converts
Replaces them with self-host-to-cloud conversion, or another indicator that sits upstream of the money and is readable on a stated cadence
Names gross margin per workload as the guardrail tracked beside it for a hosted open-source model
Attaches a target and a date to the leading indicator
Rejects competition, execution and market timing as risks because none of them carries an observable signal
Gives each risk a named signal with a threshold and the place it is read
Produces the memo with its named sections: constraints, rejected models, primary model, paid boundary, value metric, go-to-market consequence, leading indicator, risks, revisit triggers
Includes at least three revisit triggers, at least one of which is a failure condition
Presents the memo section by section and seeks agreement before continuing, instead of delivering all nine sections at once

evals.prompt: Just tell me which business model to run. Glintpad is a single-binary MIT-licensed CLI that tidies up local photo libraries. It runs entirely on the user's laptop, never touches the network, and stores nothing of ours anywhere. Our users are hobbyists; in three years not one company has ever contacted us. We will never change the licence, we've promised that publicly. There's no plugin ecosystem, nobody here could sell anything to anyone, and there is nothing we could meter even if we wanted to. Which model is the right one?
evals.expected_output: A plain statement that these constraints eliminate every archetype, each elimination carrying its blocking constraint, the conclusion that either a constraint is wrong or this is not a business yet, and no invented model to fill the gap.
expectations: Says plainly that the stated constraints eliminate every archetype, instead of forcing one to fit
States that this means either one of the constraints is wrong or the product is not a business yet
Eliminates hosted SaaS and hosted open source because nothing runs on the vendor's infrastructure and there is no operational burden to sell
Eliminates dual licensing because the permissive MIT licence provides no forcing function
Eliminates source-available because the licence change is refused and no reseller threat exists
Eliminates consumption metering because nothing is meterable
Eliminates the ecosystem take-rate because no third-party ecosystem exists
Eliminates open core, support and LTS, and OEM licensing because no organization is present to sign anything
Names which specific constraint would have to change for any model to become available
Does not invent a revenue model or recommend a hopeful one in spite of the eliminations

evals.prompt: Different question from my usual ones. Stonecourse is a platform: there's the open agent that runs on customer machines, a control plane we host, a web console, and about 30 connectors, of which we wrote 11 and the community wrote the rest. Our community keeps asking what will always be free and we keep dodging the question because we haven't settled the money side yet. What do I tell them?
evals.expected_output: An explicit always-free list produced now rather than deferred, the 19 community connectors placed on the free side, the stack mapped layer by layer with Wardley mapping attributed, the chargeable layer identified, and the promise treated as irreversible.
expectations: Produces an explicit always-free list now rather than deferring it until the revenue model is settled
States that silence about what stays free is read as intent to close, and that the community prices that in immediately
Places the 19 community-written connectors on the always-free side
Maps the stack layer by layer instead of answering at the level of the whole product
Applies Wardley mapping because the product spans several layers
Attributes Wardley mapping to Simon Wardley, created at Fotango in 2005
Describes Wardley mapping as positioning components on a value chain against an evolution axis
Locates the money one layer above the component everyone needs and nobody wants to own
Treats a public promise about what stays free forever as effectively irreversible
Identifies the hosted control plane, the layer the vendor operates, as the chargeable surface rather than gating features inside the open agent
